title: Hurricane season wrap-up: El Niño fueled record number of Pacific storms but calmed Atlantic

Credit: NOAA Satellites The 2026 hurricane season, which officially ends on Nov. 30, will be remembered as a year of contrasts between the Atlantic and Pacific, a classic indication of a hurricane season influenced by a very strong El Niño. Below-normal activity across the Atlantic basin was offset by above-average activity in the Pacific, including two disasters in Hawaii. "NOAA's unparalleled forecasting skill and scientific expertise provided the early warnings needed to protect lives and property this hurricane season," said Neil Jacobs, Ph.D., NOAA administrator. "This included accurately predicting this year's very strong El Niño months in advance, which gave us the critical insight we needed to accurately forecast this season." Atlantic basin The Atlantic basin produced 10 named storms , of which one (Isaias) became a hurricane. Isaias was also the season's only major hurricane with top sustained winds of 120 mph (193 kilometers per hour). An average season has 14 named storms (winds of 39 mph (63 kilometers per hour) or greater), seven hurricanes (winds of 74 mph (119 kilometers per hour) or greater) and three major hurricanes (winds of 111 mph (179 kilometers per hour) or greater). A summary graphic showing an alphabetical list of the 2026 Atlantic tropical cyclone names as selected by the World Meteorological Organization: Arthur, Bertha, Cristobal, Dolly, Edouard, Fay, Gonzalo, Hanna, Isaias, Josephine, Kyle, Leah, Marco, Nana, Omar, Paulette, Rene, Sally, Teddy, Vicky and Wilfred. The 2026 hurricane season, which runs June 1 through Nov. 30, saw 10 named tropical systems and ended with Josephine. Credit: NOAA NWS Tropical Storm Arthur kicked off the season, forming near the Texas coast on June 17, which is close to the average date for the first named storm of the Atlantic season to develop. Though it was a short-lived tropical storm, its remnants contributed to widespread heavy rain and flooding in the southeastern United States, along with numerous tornadoes and other severe weather. More than a month passed before the next named tropical storm, Tropical Storm Bertha, which formed on July 20 along the northern Gulf Coast. Bertha was a highly sheared tropical storm that brought gusty winds, rough surf and minor-to-moderate coastal flooding from Florida to Louisiana. The season's most notable storm, Hurricane Isaias, made landfall on Oct. 9 as a Category 2 hurricane near Destin, Florida, and was the first hurricane to make landfall in the mainland United States since Milton in October 2024. Isaias brought a significant storm surge to Panama City Beach, Florida, and damaging wind gusts over a large portion of the U.S. Southeast, in addition to flooding rain. "Despite being a relatively quiet season overall, this hurricane season was a clear example of the message we often say: It only takes one storm for it to be a bad season," said Ken Graham, director of NOAA's National Weather Service. This year's El Niño was among the strongest on record and played a key role in shaping the 2026 hurricane season. The Pacific Ocean saw an exceptional amount of hurricane activity. On the other hand, the Atlantic saw remarkably little. As hurricane season comes to a close, our new Earth from Orbit video takes a look back at the major tropical cyclones that occurred in 2026, as well as the El Niño that greatly influenced their formation.
